Grade 4 Sex Education

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Child rape statistics in South Africa are horrifying but how should our children be taught to protect themselves?

Unique Selling Point:
At the begining of the school year Kerry Steyn’s nine year old came home with her school books as disseminated by her primary school Kenridge in the Western Cape. Kenridge boasts over 2000 learners. As per instruction, the children have to cover their books in clear plastic. When it came time to cover her maths book, Kerry's nine year old daughter was stressed and confused, turned her book to the back and asked her mom what rape is? Kerry was totally unprepared for the question or why her daughter was asking these things until she saw the message on the back of the maths book which reads:

WHAT SHOULD YOU DO IF YOU ARE RAPED OR SEXUALLY ASSAULTED?

1. Go to a safe place where you can get help

2. Tell someone you trust what happened as soon as possible

3. Do not throw away your clothes or wasj yourself

4. Put the clothes you were wearing in a paper bag or wrap them in newspaper

5. Go to a hospital as soon as possible

6. It is advisable to report the rape to the police

7. Tell the police if you are threatened by the perpetrator at any time

8. Get treatment and medication within 72 hours to prevent HIV, other sexually transmitted infections and pregnancy

REMEMBER IT IS NEVER THE FAULT OF THE PERSON WHO WAS RAPED, ABUSED, VIOLATED OR HARASSED!


Summary:
Kerry's daughter is going through severe covid anxiety and this message about having to go to police and not knowing what rape or sexual assault are made the little girl very scared. When Kerry confronted the school as to why such messaging was put on the back of a maths book without any warning to parents or any lead up education by the school, they brushed it off saying she was the only one that complained, yet they had made a decision not to put up certain HIV posters around the school that the Department had provided them with, because younger children would be confused by them. Kerry is having to deal with this personally and through her daughter's psychologist. When she posted it on social media, many parents came back and said they were horrified and thought it was negligent of the school to allow such messaging and other parents from her school were also very concerned. She received a response from one of the parents at Durbanville Primary who had also seen the message at the back of the book and the school decided to have the parents cover the back with brown paper so that the message would not be seen by the classes.

Further information:
This is a story about the Department of Education in the Western Cape.

The question is, we know how serious rape and sexual assault are in South Africa, is this the way the Department of Education is choosing to inform young children of the dangers and how to deal with them? We can speak to a child psychologist about what it means for a nine year old to get their first sexual education this way, and confront the Department of Education as to what seems dangerous and negligent messaging to young children.


Case studies:

Kerry Steyn - 072 333 4296 - She is the parent who brought it to the attention of Kenridge Primary and was upset with the messaging - I have spoken to her and she is willing to participate.

Chris Penn- 082 432 7225 -father of three, his daughter was exposed to sex and porn through the sexual education... not sure if he is appropriate or what he is willing to say.

Tsitsi Mare - 078 782 6487 she's a doctor her children go to Kenridge and she was not happy with the messaging. Have left her a message she hasn't come back to me.

Anel Annendale - 083 711 5267 - Child psychologist - Western Cape - will be speaking to her tonight at 8pm.

Jill Hamilton - 2IC - Kenridge Primary - 021 976 3046 - Haven't spoken to them yet.. would need to contact her and see if they are willing to give us an interview and why they don't think it is a problem.. also what kind of life orientation education is coupled with this messaging?

Lauren - 079 515 6500 Parent from Welgemoed primary - Western Cape., same maths book the school asked the parents to cover the back page of the book. haven't spoken to her yet.. need to reflect this element of the story.

Karabo Ozah: 071 682 1761 Children's Act lawyer - Have spoken to her sent her the message and she will get back to me with comment. - maybe if I don't include her in the programme she can form one of your panelists for Chwayitisa's debate.

Department of Education, Western Cape - to address who decided to put the message on the maths book, how they evaluated it's appropriateness and how is this coupled with the sexual orientation that the children are receiving in schools?

Press Release:


Sexual abuse and rape are life-altering violations, especially for children. So the Department of Basic Education have put out a guide for nine-year-olds about what to do if they are raped. Could this response to the scourge of sexual violence do more harm than good?

Script:


Link: It's a common dilemma faced by parents, when to tell their children about the birds and the bees, about love and sex. But how do you broach the much more difficult discussion about the harsh realities of rape and sexual abuse?


Kerry:
Don't throw away your clothes or wash yourself.
Go to a hospital as soon as possible.
It is advisable to report the rape to the police.


VO: For Kerry Steyn, a vet and mother of two in the Western Cape, these are not the kind of instructions she ever thought she'd be discussing with her nine-year-old daughter.

Kerry: If anything, it's been a conversation of Mommy, what is a period… how a baby's made.


VO: Kerry's daughter attends a local government school, and while she was sick with Covid, her workbooks were sent home.


Kerry: I went into the study to go and get something to do the work with her. And when I came back, she said to me, “Mommy, what is rape?” So I was like, “sorry?” // And she said, “it's over here on the back of this book.” Her grade four maths book that's issued from the Department of Education.
Derek: How did you react?
Kerry: I was stumped. I wasn't prepared. // I said to her sweetheart, rape is a horrific crime that is committed against a person and the details of it are something far beyond your understanding of a nine-year-old.//
… So give me some time…
Derek: Did she accept that explanation?
Kerry: She did. //And then I was angry. Because why did I have to be put in that position?


VO: But it's a position that many families are having to face. A 2015 Optimus study questioned thousands of young people across South Africa. The findings were shocking - like one in three has experienced some form of sexual abuse by the age of seventeen, and boys are marginally more likely to be victims than girls. Many cases of rape and sexual assault go unreported.
Confronted with this reality, the Department of Basic Education, (DBE) wants children to be able to seek help, according to spokesperson Elijah Mhlanga.


Elijah: It's about GBV is about protecting children against sexual assault. It's about preventing learner pregnancy whose numbers are astronomical.


VO: It's also about overcoming the reluctance of many parents and caregivers across the country who are hesitant to broach these issues.


Elijah: It starts in the home, there shouldn't be anything that we call taboo, we need to really open up and start to talk to our children about it.


VO: He emphasises that awareness campaigns for its comprehensive sexuality education programme (CSE), can only do so much.


Elijah: So if a child asks, What is rape? answer the question, the question is, are you equipped to do that? If not, seek help yourself. In the real world, children are actually sexually active and parents are in denial.


VO: Kerry doesn't believe she's in denial, but rather that the message was too harsh, too soon, for her nine-year-old.


Derek: It's phrased in a very adult fashion
Kerry: It's very adult and it's fearful. And that's my nine-year-old asking me “when will I be raped?”
Derek: Ja


VO: The school told Kerry they were unaware of the message on the book, that no one else had complained, and referred it to the Department.


Derek: We can't get away from the fact that this nine-year-old girl was traumatised and confused
Elijah: But then explain to them that they are growing up, it is probably even better that she came across information which talks about rape, she could have been raped herself.


LINK: Is there a perfect age to tell your child about the terrifying concepts of rape and sexual assault?

Monty: We thought of starting with the Grade 4's, which is about 9, 8/9 years old because we had incidents of learners that was 10/11 who fell pregnant.


VO: Monty Sandows has been an integral part of Dowling Primary school in Westbury Johannesburg, for 42 years - as a learner, a teacher, and now as its headmaster.


Monty: We continuously deal with issues of learners informing us that, you know, they were either sexually molested at home, or in the community. We try and ensure that they at least inform us at the school so that we can intervene before it happens.


VO: But even in a community plagued by gangsterism, drug and alcohol abuse that escalate these problems, this headmaster felt uncomfortable with some of the tough messaging.


Monty: How do you talk about rape to a 9 and 10-year-old, You have to gently nudge them into the direction as to what does it really mean? Even the bigger ones, you can't just talk about rape, it's a process.


VO: And that's how Kerry says she felt - that there had been no process. She posted her concerns online and there was immediate support from her social groups.


Derek: Many parents didn't think it was appropriate that such a harshly worded message was put on a maths book.
Elijah: No, that message is not harsh at all. Opinion is an opinion. It was mediated it was approved. It is based on consultation with communities. It is what parents elsewhere have asked for.


LINK: So why do some parents fear talking to their children? Could they possibly be trying to preserve their innocence at the expense of their safety?


VO: Social worker Edith Kriel is the Executive Director of Jelly Beanz, an organisation centred on ending child abuse and trauma around the country.


Edith: It's very important for children to have an understanding of sexuality in the bigger context. So not only looking at when things can go wrong but also what is sexuality and positive sexuality. And we believe these conversations need to start from a young age.


VO: Because Jelly Beanz produces reading material that educates children around sexuality, we asked Kriel to give us her opinion on how easily a nine-year-old could follow the instructions on the maths book.


Edith: if I just look at some of the wording, remember, it's never the fault of the person who was raped, abused, violated, or harassed. Even you and I might look at them and go, what's the difference between abuse, harassment, and violation? The whole essence of this awareness page is very cold and clinical, there is no context to looking at children should be protected. Now, we are asking young children to do things that shouldn't be the responsibility of children.


VO: Nonverbal messaging, like the design and what colours are used, is equally critical according to Kriel.


Edith: So there is a hand which is meant to be a hand saying let's stop rape.
Derek: Yeah.
Edith: But for many of our children, that hand is a hurtful hand because children are exposed to physical violence all of the time. If you have a look at the section, which talks about what you’re meant to do, if you've been sexually abused, the background colour is a block of dark red. That is the colour of blood


VO: But the department is determined - even at primary school level - every child should get the message.


Elijah: If you look at that cover, there's a number there. It says, if you are sexually violated, this is what you need to do.


VO: We decided to do just that, and called all the numbers listed on the cover.


Edith: This is the old childline number.
Speaker: Our number is changing to 116 soon please hold and you'll be directed to a counsellor who will help you.
Speaker: Sorry - the network is congested.
Derek: And cut off.
Edith: We've got the Department of Basic Education national hotline.
Speaker: Sorry - the dialled number is not in service.
Edith: SAPS crime stop.
Speaker: Please select one of the following options
Derek: Very complicated for a child.
Edith: Traumatised, abused and afraid...
Derek: That is not gonna work.
Edith: This the SAPS emergency number
Derek: 10111?
Edith: That's correct.
Derek: This is not good.
Edith: There’s not even a message.
Derek: I'm absolutely appalled.
Edith: I must be very honest, I didn't expect that. Children will not believe that they are safe or protected after this.


VO: Now let's see what happens if we call the correct number for childline - 116.


Sound up: Childline: Good afternoon, you’ve reached Childline. How can I help?
Derek: Good afternoon.
VO: And the operator answers immediately.
Derek: So if you give the right number, you do get response.
END PHONE CALL MONTAGE


Derek: Edith should the department retract this message, is it doing more harm than good?
Edith: It's out there and potentially may be helpful to some children, but can we then provide the context?


VO: The DBE insists it is providing the context, with workshops and a strict script around comprehensive sexuality education for teachers. But all schools may not be sticking to it. Kerry Steyn still feels left out in the cold, but on the other hand, it has given her serious pause for thought.


Kerry: I was unprepared for this. And given the relevance that it has brought, It has been a huge wake-up call for me and for our family, that this is something that we're going to have to be educating sooner than what we anticipated.

If you have a look at the section, which talks about what you’re meant to do, if you've been sexually abused, the background colour is a block of dark red. That is the colour of blood VO: But the department is determined - even at primary school level - every child should get the message. Elijah: If you look at that cover, there's a number there. It says, if you are sexually violated, this is what you need to do. VO: We decided to do just that, and called all the numbers listed on the cover. Edith: This is the old childline number. Speaker: Our number is changing to 116 soon please hold and you'll be directed to a counsellor who will help you. Speaker: Sorry - the network is congested. Derek: And cut off. Edith: We've got the Department of Basic Education national hotline. Speaker: Sorry - the dialled number is not in service. Edith: SAPS crime stop. Speaker: Please select one of the following options Derek: Very complicated for a child. Edith: Traumatised, abused and afraid... Derek: That is not gonna work. Edith: This the SAPS emergency number Derek: 10111? Edith: That's correct. Derek: This is not good. Edith: There’s not even a message. Derek: I'm absolutely appalled. Edith: I must be very honest, I didn't expect that. Children will not believe that they are safe or protected after this. VO: Now let's see what happens if we call the correct number for childline - 116. Sound up: Childline: Good afternoon, you’ve reached Childline. How can I help? Derek: Good afternoon. VO: And the operator answers immediately. Derek: So if you give the right number, you do get response. END PHONE CALL MONTAGE Derek: Edith should the department retract this message, is it doing more harm than good? Edith: It's out there and potentially may be helpful to some children, but can we then provide the context? VO: The DBE insists it is providing the context, with workshops and a strict script around comprehensive sexuality education for teachers. But all schools may not be sticking to it. Kerry Steyn still feels left out in the cold, but on the other hand, it has given her serious pause for thought. Kerry: I was unprepared for this. And given the relevance that it has brought, It has been a huge wake-up call for me and for our family, that this is something that we're going to have to be educating sooner than what we anticipated.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Child rape statistics in South Africa are horrifying but how should our children be taught to protect themselves?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: At the begining of the school year Kerry Steyn’s nine year old came home with her school books as disseminated by her primary school Kenridge in the Western Cape. Kenridge boasts over 2000 learners. As per instruction, the children have to cover their books in clear plastic. When it came time to cover her maths book, Kerry's nine year old daughter was stressed and confused, turned her book to the back and asked her mom what rape is? Kerry was totally unprepared for the question or why her daughter was asking these things until she saw the message on the back of the maths book which reads: WHAT SHOULD YOU DO IF YOU ARE RAPED OR SEXUALLY ASSAULTED? 1. Go to a safe place where you can get help 2. Tell someone you trust what happened as soon as possible 3. Do not throw away your clothes or wasj yourself 4. Put the clothes you were wearing in a paper bag or wrap them in newspaper 5. Go to a hospital as soon as possible 6. It is advisable to report the rape to the police 7. Tell the police if you are threatened by the perpetrator at any time 8. Get treatment and medication within 72 hours to prevent HIV, other sexually transmitted infections and pregnancy REMEMBER IT IS NEVER THE FAULT OF THE PERSON WHO WAS RAPED, ABUSED, VIOLATED OR HARASSED!
metadata.Summary: Kerry's daughter is going through severe covid anxiety and this message about having to go to police and not knowing what rape or sexual assault are made the little girl very scared. When Kerry confronted the school as to why such messaging was put on the back of a maths book without any warning to parents or any lead up education by the school, they brushed it off saying she was the only one that complained, yet they had made a decision not to put up certain HIV posters around the school that the Department had provided them with, because younger children would be confused by them. Kerry is having to deal with this personally and through her daughter's psychologist. When she posted it on social media, many parents came back and said they were horrified and thought it was negligent of the school to allow such messaging and other parents from her school were also very concerned. She received a response from one of the parents at Durbanville Primary who had also seen the message at the back of the book and the school decided to have the parents cover the back with brown paper so that the message would not be seen by the classes.
metadata.Further information: This is a story about the Department of Education in the Western Cape. The question is, we know how serious rape and sexual assault are in South Africa, is this the way the Department of Education is choosing to inform young children of the dangers and how to deal with them? We can speak to a child psychologist about what it means for a nine year old to get their first sexual education this way, and confront the Department of Education as to what seems dangerous and negligent messaging to young children.
